formation.title: The Kingdom of the Deccan
formation.text:
Two hundred years the plateau answered to Delhi, and answered late. The roads north climb the Vindhyas and then run a thousand miles through country the sultans had to reconquer every reign; Muhammad bin Tughluq moved his whole court to Daulatabad to hold it and then moved it back again, and the amirs he left behind learned what the distance was worth.

Now the khutba is read in our name and the coin is struck in it. The green banner goes up over the double moat at Gulbarga, and the fifteen towers answer it. But a name is not a state, and the men who raised us are already asking what the raising was for. The amirs of the tarafs want the country they hold confirmed to them. The court wants Persians for the guns and the ledgers, and the sea at Dabhol is close enough to fetch them by the shipload.

Both are how a Deccan sultanate is built. Only one of them is how ours will be.

modifiers.name: The Amirs of the Tarafs
modifiers.text: The sultanate is governed through the men who made it. Each taraf answers to its own amir, raises its own horse from its own villages, and feeds its own troops from its own harvest. Nothing reaches the throne that the provinces do not send.

options.text: Send to Bidar for better men

modifiers.name: The Court of Bidar
modifiers.text: The court buys what the plateau cannot raise. Gunners out of Anatolia, physicians and secretaries out of Iran, and the ships at Dabhol to bring them. The offices fill with men who were not born here, and the amirs who were are counting.

advances.name: Sultanate Foundations
advances.text: The Bahmani Sultanate, born from rebellion against Delhi's distant rule, established the first independent Muslim state on the Deccan Plateau. Under Ala-ud-Din Hasan Bahman Shah, the new dynasty claimed legitimacy and centralized authority across its vast domains.

advances.name: Gulbarga Fortifications
advances.text: The great fortress at Gulbarga, ringed by a double moat and fifteen towers, served as the impregnable heart of the early Bahmani state. Its walls sheltered the first capital and projected Sultanate power across the western Deccan.

advances.name: Persianate Court
advances.text: The Bahmani court consciously modeled itself on Persian traditions, importing scholars, poets, and administrators from Iran and Central Asia. The darbar hall became a center of refined culture where Persian etiquette governed affairs of state.

advances.name: Deccani Horsemen
advances.text: The Bahmani sultans invested heavily in cavalry, importing Arabian and Persian horses through the western ports. Mounted sowars formed the striking arm of the Sultanate's armies across the Deccan plateau.

advances.name: Arabian Horse Trade
advances.text: Control of the western coast ports like Chaul and later Goa gave the Bahmanis direct access to the Arabian horse trade. These imports sustained the Sultanate's cavalry superiority over their Vijayanagara rivals.

advances.name: Bahmani Legal Code
advances.text: The early Bahmani sultans established a systematic legal framework drawing on Islamic jurisprudence and Persian administrative tradition, bringing order to the governance of their diverse domains.

advances.name: Deccan Plateau Agriculture
advances.text: The black soil of the Deccan Plateau, enriched by seasonal monsoons, supported extensive agriculture. Cotton, millet, and pulses fed the Sultanate's growing population and fueled its economy.

advances.name: Gawan's Administrative Reforms
advances.text: The great vizier Mahmud Gawan reorganized the Bahmani state into eight provinces, each under a tarafdar with fixed responsibilities. His reforms curtailed noble power and strengthened central authority over tax collection and military affairs.

event.title: The Reforms of Mahmud Gawan
event.text:
Mahmud Gawan, the brilliant Persian-born vizier who has served the Sultanate for decades, has implemented sweeping administrative reforms. The kingdom's four provinces have been reorganized into eight tarafs, each under a centrally appointed tarafdar. Noble estates have been curtailed, revenues systematized, and the Sultanate's magnificent madrasa at Bidar stands as a monument to his vision.

Yet these reforms have deepened the fault line at the heart of the Bahmani state. The Afaqi nobles (Persians, Turks, and Arabs who followed Gawan to power) now hold sway at court. The Deccani nobles, born of this soil, seethe at their displacement. The Sultan must choose which faction's path to follow.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Strengthen central authority: the tarafs shall answer to the throne.

modifiers.name: Gawan's Centralization
modifiers.text: The great vizier's reforms have strengthened central authority, curtailing provincial autonomy and systematizing revenue collection across the tarafs.

options.text: Embrace Gawan's cosmopolitan vision: let the world come to our court.

modifiers.name: Gawan's Cosmopolitan Vision
modifiers.text: Mahmud Gawan's policy of tolerance and his patronage of scholars from diverse backgrounds has enriched the court and broadened the Sultanate's diplomatic horizons.

advances.name: Mahmud Gawan Madrasa
advances.text: The magnificent madrasa at Bidar, built by Mahmud Gawan in 1472, stood three stories tall with a library of three thousand manuscripts. It became a beacon of Islamic scholarship, drawing students and scholars from across the Muslim world.

advances.name: Bidriware Metalwork
advances.text: Under Bahmani patronage, artisans in Bidar perfected a unique metalworking technique, casting zinc-copper alloy vessels, then inlaying them with silver in intricate arabesque patterns. Blackened with a soil paste mixed with ammonium chloride, the finished pieces became prized across the Indian Ocean world.

event.title: The Art of Bidri
event.text:
Under the patronage of the Sultanate, artisans in Bidar have perfected a metalworking technique of extraordinary beauty and skill. Vessels are cast from an alloy of zinc and copper, then engraved with intricate designs, arabesques, calligraphy, flowers, and geometric patterns. Pure silver wire is hammered into the grooves, and the surface is treated with a paste of soil and ammonium chloride unique to the soil of Bidar itself.

The result is striking: blackened metal adorned with gleaming silver, pieces that are both functional vessels and works of art. Already, Bidriware is prized by collectors and merchants from Persia to Southeast Asia. It is a craft that could only have been born here, on the Deccan, where Persian metalworking traditions met Indian artistry and Bidar's unique soil.

options.text: A treasure of the Deccan that shall endure for centuries.

advances.name: Deccan Gunpowder
advances.text: The Bahmani Sultanate was likely the first Indian state to employ gunpowder artillery. By the 1460s, the fortress of Kalyana had gun ports built into its walls, and topchi gunners served in every major campaign.

event.title: Thunder on the Deccan
event.text:
The fortress of Kalyana stands as proof of the Sultanate's military revolution. Gun ports have been built directly into its walls, the first such design anywhere on the Deccan Plateau. The sound of cannon fire, once alien to this land, now echoes across the plateau as our topchi gunners drill with their fearsome weapons.

The Bahmani Sultanate has become the first Indian state to systematically employ gunpowder artillery. Our fire-workers can breach any wall, our cannons can break any charge. The military balance of the Deccan has shifted forever. Where once the outcome of battle depended on the weight of cavalry, now it depends on the thunder of guns, and our guns speak loudest of all.

options.text: Let the thunder of our guns proclaim Bahmani supremacy.

advances.name: Port of Dabhol
advances.text: The capture of Dabhol and later Goa gave the Bahmanis direct access to maritime trade with Persia, Arabia, and East Africa. These ports became conduits for horse imports, luxury goods, and Persian cultural influence.

advances.name: Persian Literary Court
advances.text: The Bahmani court cultivated Persian as the language of administration and high culture. Poets, historians, and scholars from Iran found patronage at Gulbarga and Bidar, creating a vibrant Persianate literary tradition on Indian soil.

advances.name: Caravanserai Network
advances.text: A network of caravanserais along major trade routes provided secure lodging, water, and protection for merchants crossing the Deccan. These rest houses facilitated overland commerce and helped bind the Sultanate's far-flung provinces.

advances.name: Wars Against Vijayanagara
advances.text: The struggle between the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire defined a century of Deccani history. Control of the Raichur Doab, the fertile land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, was the perpetual prize worth fighting for.

event.title: The Wars Against Vijayanagara
event.text:
The struggle between the Sultanate and the great Hindu empire of Vijayanagara has defined a generation. The fertile Raichur Doab, the land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, is the perpetual prize, changing hands with the fortunes of war. Our topchi gunners have proven their worth against Vijayanagara's mighty cavalry, and the siege of Belgaum demonstrated that no fortress can long withstand the Bahmani's fire-workers.

The question now is how to consolidate our gains. Do we press the advantage with offensive power, or fortify the frontier against inevitable counterattack?

options.text: Press the attack: the sword of the Deccan shall not rest.

modifiers.name: Sword of the Deccan
modifiers.text: Victory on the battlefield has steeled the Sultanate's resolve. Our armies are battle-hardened, our artillery feared, and our siege craft proven against the mightiest fortresses.

options.text: Fortify the frontier: no enemy shall breach our bastions.

modifiers.name: Shield of the Plateau
modifiers.text: The lessons of perpetual warfare have been turned to defense. Our fortresses bristle with cannon, our garrisons are disciplined, and our frontier positions are impregnable.

advances.name: Siege Artillery Corps
advances.text: Under Mahmud Gawan's command, the Bahmanis developed specialized siege techniques including mining and directed cannon fire. During the siege of Belgaum in 1472, dedicated fire-workers breached fortifications using methods never before seen on the Deccan.

advances.name: Afaqi-Deccani Balance
advances.text: The Sultanate was perpetually divided between Afaqi nobles (foreign-born Persians, Turks, and Arabs who held court influence) and Deccanis, locally born Muslims and Habshi freedmen who controlled the provinces. Managing this balance was the central challenge of Bahmani statecraft.

event.title: The Afaqi-Deccani Crisis
event.text:
The tension that has simmered at the heart of the Sultanate for generations has reached a critical juncture. The Afaqis (foreign-born nobles from Persia, Turkey, and Arabia) control the court, the treasury, and the diplomatic service. They speak Persian, correspond with the courts of Isfahan and Constantinople, and maintain the commercial networks that bring horses, luxury goods, and recruits to the Sultanate.

The Deccanis (locally born Muslims, converts, and Habshi freedmen from Abyssinia) control the provinces, command the garrisons, and draw their strength from the land itself. They speak Dakhani, know the terrain, and command the loyalty of the common soldier.

Both factions have served the Sultanate, but both cannot rule it. The Sultan must decide which faction's vision will shape the Bahmani future.

options.text: The Afaqis: their Persian connections enrich us all.

modifiers.name: Afaqi Ascendancy
modifiers.text: The foreign-born nobles have prevailed, bringing their Persian connections, commercial networks, and cosmopolitan worldview to the forefront of Sultanate affairs.

options.text: The Deccanis: our strength lies in the soil we stand on.

modifiers.name: Deccani Roots
modifiers.text: The locally-born nobility has secured its position, rooting the Sultanate firmly in the soil of the Deccan. Their deep ties to the land ensure stability and plentiful levies.

advances.name: Deccan Textile Trade
advances.text: The Deccan's cotton weaving traditions produced fine textiles sought after across the Indian Ocean world. The Sultanate's control of both the production centers and the western coastal ports made textiles a cornerstone of Bahmani prosperity. Its own cloth was himroo, cotton and silk woven together at Daulatabad by weavers who had come south with the Tughluq court and stayed.

advances.name: Polygon Bastions
advances.text: Adapting to the gunpowder age, Bahmani military engineers designed fortifications with angular bastions capable of mounting cannons in overlapping fields of fire. By the 1460s, these innovations had transformed the Deccan's defensive landscape.

advances.name: Sultanate Diplomacy
advances.text: The Bahmani sultans maintained diplomatic connections across the Islamic world, exchanging ambassadors with the Mamluks, Timurids, and Ottoman Empire. These relationships provided military recruits, cultural exchange, and political legitimacy.

advances.name: Successor State Legacy
advances.text: Though the Bahmani state fragmented after 1518, its administrative traditions, military innovations, and cultural achievements lived on in the successor sultanates. The institutions Mahmud Gawan built proved more durable than the dynasty itself.

advances.name: Tofangchi Musketeers
advances.text: Trained matchlock infantry became a staple of Deccani armies. These tofangchi, many recruited from Persian and Central Asian immigrants, brought disciplined firearm tactics to the battlefield.

advances.name: Diamond Mining
advances.text: The Deccan Plateau held some of the world's most productive diamond deposits. The Golconda mines yielded stones of legendary quality, including what would later become known as the Hope Diamond and the Koh-i-Noor.

advances.name: Deccani Miniature Painting
advances.text: A distinctive school of miniature painting flourished in the Deccan sultanates, blending Persian, Indian, and even European influences into a uniquely Deccani aesthetic marked by bold colors and fantastical imagery.

advances.name: Revenue Taraf System
advances.text: The Bahmani provincial revenue system divided the realm into tarafs, each with systematized tax collection overseen by centrally appointed officials. This framework, refined across generations, ensured a steady flow of revenue to the Sultanate treasury.

advances.name: Deccani Syncretism
advances.text: Centuries of Muslim and Hindu coexistence on the Deccan produced a distinctive syncretic culture. Sufi saints attracted Hindu devotees, temple dancers performed in Muslim courts, and shared festivals blurred the boundaries between communities.

advances.name: Nizam Administration
advances.text: The administrative traditions of the Bahmani state found their fullest expression in the Nizam-ul-Mulk's governance. Systematic bureaucracy, regular revenue assessment, and provincial organization maintained order across the Deccan.

advances.name: European Military Contact
advances.text: Contact with European military advisors and merchants introduced new techniques in drill, fortification design, and artillery deployment. Deccani rulers selectively adopted these innovations to modernize their armed forces.

advances.name: Deccani Water Works
advances.text: Elaborate stepped wells, aqueducts, and irrigation channels engineered across the Deccan brought water to arid regions and sustained agricultural expansion. These public works represented significant state investment in infrastructure.

advances.name: Reformed Sipahi
advances.text: Adapting to the changing nature of warfare, Deccani heavy cavalry underwent reform. The reformed sipahi combined traditional shock tactics with pistol-armed tactics suited to the gunpowder battlefield.

advances.name: Deccani Trade Maturity
advances.text: By the age of absolutism, the Deccan's commercial networks had matured into a sophisticated system of overland and maritime trade routes connecting the interior plateau to the coasts and beyond.

advances.name: Modern Administration
advances.text: Enlightenment-era administrative reforms brought systematized record-keeping, regularized taxation, and rationalized provincial governance to the successor states of the Bahmani tradition.

advances.name: Deccani Cultural Legacy
advances.text: The cultural achievements of the Bahmani era (Bidri ware, Deccani miniature painting, Persian-influenced architecture, and the Dakhani literary tradition) endured as a lasting legacy of Deccani civilization.

advances.name: Cultural Synthesis
advances.text: The long coexistence of Muslim, Hindu, and other traditions on the Deccan produced a cultural synthesis unique in the subcontinent, enriching music, cuisine, language, and the arts with hybrid forms.

advances.name: Industrial Workshops
advances.text:
The Deccan's traditional textile crafts and metalworking traditions provided a foundation for early industrial workshops, as mechanized cotton processing and metal fabrication emerged.

Available in: Himroo Looms

advances.name: Modern Field Guns
advances.text: Building on centuries of gunpowder expertise, Deccani arsenals produced modern field artillery incorporating European design principles with local manufacturing capability.

units.name: Deccani Sowar
units.text: Mounted cavalry on imported Arabian horses, the Deccani sowars were the striking arm of the Bahmani armies. Fast, disciplined, and bred for the open plateau, they dominated the battlefield.

units.name: Topchi
units.text: The earliest gunpowder artillery corps in the Indian subcontinent. Bahmani topchi gunners manned cannons imported from or inspired by Ottoman and Persian designs, bringing devastating firepower to siege and field.

units.name: Siege Topchi
units.text: Specialized siege artillery teams who combined cannon fire with mining operations. Under Mahmud Gawan's command, these engineers breached fortifications using techniques never before employed on the Deccan.

units.name: Tofangchi
units.text: Trained matchlock infantry, many recruited from Persian and Central Asian immigrants. The tofangchi brought disciplined volley fire to the Deccani battlefield, supplementing the Sultanate's traditional cavalry arm.

units.name: Reformed Sipahi
units.text: Heavy cavalry reformed for the gunpowder era, combining the shock charge tradition with pistol-armed tactics. These elite horsemen served as the decisive arm in the later Deccani wars.

units.name: Deccani Field Gun
units.text: Modern field artillery drawing on centuries of Deccani gunpowder expertise. Lighter and more mobile than siege pieces, these guns provided devastating battlefield firepower.

buildings.name: Qila
buildings.text: A Deccan hilltop fortress in the Bahmani tradition, built from local basalt and designed to withstand prolonged siege. Its towers and walls command the surrounding plateau.

buildings.name: Darbar Hall
buildings.text: A court hall built in the Persian tradition, where the Sultan holds audience and affairs of state are conducted according to the refined etiquette of the Persianate court.

buildings.name: Taraf Office
buildings.text: A provincial administrative center implementing Mahmud Gawan's reforms, where appointed officials manage tax collection, military levies, and correspondence with the central court.

buildings.name: Madrasa
buildings.text: An Islamic center of learning modeled on Mahmud Gawan's magnificent madrasa at Bidar. Students study theology, law, mathematics, and astronomy under scholars drawn from across the Islamic world.

buildings.name: Bidri Workshop
buildings.text: A specialized metalworking atelier where artisans practice the Bidriware technique, casting zinc-copper alloy vessels, engraving intricate designs, and inlaying them with pure silver before blackening the surface.

buildings.name: Bandargah
buildings.text: A coastal trading port in the Bahmani tradition, facilitating maritime commerce with Persia, Arabia, and East Africa. Warehouses, customs offices, and merchant quarters line the waterfront.

buildings.name: Sarai
buildings.text: A walled court on the road with a well, a mosque and stabling, a day's march from the next. Merchants and their pack trains lodge here on the way between the ports and the capital.

where.text: Joined to the capital by road

buildings.name: Himroo Looms
buildings.text: Looms where a cotton warp is woven under a silk weft into himroo, a cloth made to look like Persian brocade at a fraction of its price.

where.text: Cotton is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Diamond Diggings
buildings.text: Shallow pits sunk into the river gravels of Golconda. The gravel is carried out in baskets, washed, dried and picked over by hand, and more of the stones the ground holds are found.

where.text: The location's raw material is Gems

buildings.name: Polygon Bastion
buildings.text: An angular fortification designed for the gunpowder age, with bastions that provide overlapping fields of cannon fire. These Deccani innovations preceded similar European developments.

buildings.name: Revenue Office
buildings.text: A provincial revenue collection center where officials assess taxes, maintain land records, and remit revenue to the central treasury according to the taraf system.

buildings.name: Baoli
buildings.text: A stepped well engineered to access the Deccan's deep water table. These monumental structures serve as public water sources, cool retreats, and gathering places.

list.name: Wakil-us-Sultanat
list.text: The Wakil-us-Sultanat was the Bahmani sultan's vicegerent, a single great office that combined household management, the inspectorate of the cavalry rolls, and command of the central army when the sultan did not march in person. Hasan Gangu staffed it with Iranian and Iraqi emigres rather than Tughluq carryovers; Muhammad Shah I used it to lead the campaigns against Vijayanagara and Telingana. Concentrating war, household and inspectorate functions in one office gave the early Bahmanis their cohesion, and made the Wakil's office the real prize of every faction fight in Gulbarga.

list.name: Madrasa Mahmud Gawan
list.text: Completed at Bidar in 1472, the three-storey Madrasa Mahmud Gawan was the largest scholarly endowment in the Indian sultanates of the fifteenth century. Its plan (a courtyard ringed by 100 student cells, two minarets, library, mosque, and lecture-halls) was modelled on the Khargird madrasa of Khurasan; its faculty included scholars Gawan recruited personally from Samarkand, Shiraz and Herat. The library, said to hold three thousand manuscripts, was the largest in southern India before its powder magazine exploded in 1696.

list.name: Sufi Tariqa Patronage
list.text: The Chishti master Sayyid Muhammad al-Husayni Gesudaraz arrived at Gulbarga in 1397 at the invitation of Firuz Shah Bahmani; his dargah, built around his death-place in 1422, became the pilgrimage centre of the Deccan Sufi establishment. Around it the Bahmanis patronized Junaidi shrines at Daulatabad, Qadiri lodges at Bidar after 1430, and the Shattari order in Mandu. Endowing waqfs to these tariqas anchored the sultanate's legitimacy among Deccani Muslims; Bahmani sultans were buried alongside their shaykhs at Khuldabad and Gulbarga, not in court mausolea.

list.name: Daulatabad Royal Mint
list.text: Bahmani gold tankas and silver dirhams were struck principally at Daulatabad, with subsidiary mints at Gulbarga and, after 1430, Bidar. The mint-output paid the Arabian horse-trade through Goa, Chaul and Dabhol (the indispensable pipeline for the cavalry the Bahmanis fielded against Vijayanagara and Khandesh) and underwrote the Pardesi cavalry stipends that bound Iranian and Iraqi nobles to the throne. The standardized tanka, weight-controlled to the dirham of the Caliphate, gave Bahmani currency Indian Ocean acceptance.
